topic.name: The Shell Method: Rotating a Region Between Two Curves About the X-Axis

question.text: Consider the region bounded by the curves $x=3y-y^2$ and $y=\sqrt{2x},$ as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
First, we write the second function in terms $y$: \begin{align*} y &= \sqrt{2x} \\[3pt] y^2 &= 2x \\[3pt] x&=\dfrac{1}{2}y^2. \end{align*}

Now, let $f(y)=3y-y^2$ and $g(y)=\dfrac{1}{2}y^2.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f(y) &= g(y) \\[3pt] 3y-y^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2}y^2 \\[3pt] 3y-\dfrac{3}{2}y^2 &= 0 \\[3pt] \dfrac{3}{2}y(2-y) &= 0 \\[3pt] y &= 0,2 \end{align*}

So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=2.$

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function $x=g(y)=\dfrac{1}{2}y^2,$ and

  • leaves through the right function $x=f(y)=3y-y^2.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

\begin{align*} V &= 2\pi \int_{c}^{d} y \big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{right}} \big] - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{left}} \big] \big) \:\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{2} y\left( [{\color{brown}3y-y^2}] - \left[{\color{blue}\dfrac{1}{2}y^2}\right] \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{2} y\left( 3y-\dfrac{3}{2}y^2 \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{2} \left( 3y^2-\dfrac{3}{2}y^3 \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left(3 \int_{0}^{2} y^2 \:\textrm{d}y - \dfrac{3}{2}\int_{0}^{2} y^3 \textrm{d}y \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( \left.3\cdot\dfrac{y^3}{3}\right|_{0}^{2} - \left.\dfrac{3}{2}\cdot\dfrac{y^4}{4}\right|_{0}^{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( 3\left(\dfrac{8}{3}-0\right) - \dfrac{3}{2}\left(\dfrac{16}{4}-0\right) \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( 8 - 6 \right) \\[5pt] &= 4\pi \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Volume of a Solid Using the Shell Method

question.text: Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=3y-y^2$ and $x=3-y,$ as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
First, let $f(y)=3y-y^2$ and $g(y)=3-y.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f(y) &= g(y) \\[3pt] 3y-y^2 &= 3-y \\[3pt] y^2-4y+3 &= 0 \\[3pt] (y-1)(y-3) &= 0 \end{align*}

The solutions in our region are $y=1$ and $y=3.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=1$ to $y=3.$

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function $x=g(y)=3-y,$ and

  • leaves through the right function $x=f(y)=3y-y^2.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

\begin{align*} V &= 2\pi \int_{c}^{d} y \big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{right}} \big] - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{left}} \big] \big) \:\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{1}^{3} y\left( [{\color{brown}3y-y^2}] - [{\color{blue}3-y}] \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{1}^{3} y \left( -3+4y-y^2 \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] \end{align*}

example.title: Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid

question.text: Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=2y-y^2$ and $x=y,$ as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
First, let $f(y)=2y-y^2$ and $g(y)=y.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f(y) &= g(y) \\[3pt] 2y-y^2 &= y \\[3pt] y-y^2 &= 0 \\[3pt] y(1-y) &= 0 \end{align*}

The solutions are $y=0$ and $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function $x=g(y)=y,$ and

  • leaves through the right function $x=f(y)=2y-y^2.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

\begin{align*} V &= 2\pi \int_{c}^{d} y \big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{right}} \big] - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{left}} \big] \big) \:\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{1} y\left( [{\color{brown}2y-y^2}] - [{\color{blue}y}] \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{1} y \left( y-y^2 \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] \end{align*}

example.title: Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid

question.text: Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=\sqrt{y},$ $y=3-2x,$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
First, we write the second function in terms $y$: \begin{align*} y&=3-2x \\[3pt] x&=-\dfrac{1}{2}y + \dfrac{3}{2}. \end{align*}

Now, let $f(y)=\sqrt{y}$ and $g(y)=-\dfrac{1}{2}y + \dfrac{3}{2}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f(y) &= g(y) \\[3pt] \sqrt{y} &=-\dfrac{1}{2}y + \dfrac{3}{2} \\[3pt] 2\sqrt{y} &= -y + 3 \\[3pt] 4y &= 9- 6y + y^2 \\[3pt] y^2 -10y + 9 & =0\\[3pt] (y-9)(y-1) & =0 \\[3pt] y& = 1,9 \end{align*}

Checking these two solutions, we reject $y=9$ because it does not satisfy the original equation.

Therefore, the solution corresponding to our region is $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function $x=f(y)=\sqrt{y},$ and

  • leaves through the right function $x=g(y)=-\dfrac{1}{2}y + \dfrac{3}{2}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

\begin{align*} V &= 2\pi \int_{c}^{d} y \big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{right}} \big] - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{left}} \big] \big) \:\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{1} y\left(\left [{\color{brown}-\dfrac{1}{2}y + \dfrac{3}{2}}\right] - [{\color{blue}\sqrt{y}}] \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{1} \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}y^2 + \dfrac{3}{2}y - y\sqrt{y} \right)\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( -\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1} y^2 \:\textrm{d}y +\dfrac{3}{2} \int_{0}^{1} y \textrm{d}y - \int_{0}^{1} y^{3/2} \textrm{d}y \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( \left.-\dfrac{y^3}{6}\right|_{0}^{1} + \left.\dfrac{3y^2}{4}\right|_{0}^{1} - \left. \dfrac{2y^{5/2}}{5}\right|_{0}^{1}\right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( \left(-\dfrac{1}{6}-0\right) + \left(\dfrac{3}{4}-0\right) - \left(\dfrac{2}{5} - 0 \right)\right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( -\dfrac{1}{6}+ \dfrac{3}{4} - \dfrac{2}{5}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{11\pi}{30}. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Volume of a Solid Using the Shell Method

question.text: Consider the region bounded by the curves $x=6+2y-y^2,$ $x=3y^2,$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. Calculate the volume $V$ of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Now, let $f(y)=6+2y-y^2$ and $g(y)=3y^2.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y{:}$ \begin{align*} f(y) &= g(y) \\[5pt] 6+2y-y^2 &= 3y^2 \\[5pt] 6+2y-4y^2 &= 0 \\[5pt] 4y^2-2y-6 &= 0 \\[5pt] (2y-3)(y+1) &= 0 \\[5pt] y &= -1,\dfrac{3}{2} \end{align*}

The solution corresponding to our region is $y=\dfrac 3 2.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\dfrac 3 2.$

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function $x=g(y)=3y^2,$ and

  • leaves through the right function $x=f(y)=6+2y-y^2.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

\begin{align*} V &= 2\pi \int_{c}^{d} y \big( \big[ {\color{brown}\text{right}} \big] - \big[ {\color{blue}\text{left}} \big] \big) \:\textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{3/2} y\left( [{\color{brown}6+2y-y^2}] -[{\color{blue}3y^2}] \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{3/2} y\left( 6+2y-4y^2 \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \int_{0}^{3/2} \left( 6y+2y^2-4y^3 \right) \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( 6\int_{0}^{3/2} y\:\textrm{d}y+2 \int_{0}^{3/2} y^2 \:\textrm{d}y -4\int_{0}^{3/2} y^3 \textrm{d}y \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( \left.6\cdot\dfrac{y^2}{2}\right|_{0}^{3/2} + \left.2\cdot\dfrac{y^3}{3}\right|_{0}^{3/2} - \left.4\cdot\dfrac{y^4}{4}\right|_{0}^{3/2} \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( 6\left(\dfrac{9}{8}-0\right)+2\left(\dfrac{9}{8}-0\right) - \left(\dfrac{81}{16}-0\right) \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( \dfrac{27}{4}+\dfrac{9}{4}-\dfrac{81}{16} \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \left( \dfrac{63}{16} \right) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{63\pi}{8}} \end{align*}
